status: Two source-fit comparison designs account for the actual own-life and environmental duties using unchanged knowledge claims. Historical reconstruction is explicitly part of assessment success and near-miss checks; no observed pupil attainment or complete individual routine is claimed.

qilakitsoq-youngpeople.supported: Qilakitsoq near Uummannaq, northwest Greenland, around 1475; two boys in the family group, preserved skins/clothing.
qilakitsoq-youngpeople.limits: Use a respectful original text-only clothing/context summary. No remains image or mortuary/ceremonial performance required. Do not invent death causes, exact daily routines, all-Inuit clothing rules or a particular child’s school/work schedule. Keep this Greenland young-person evidence separate from Qariaraqyuk’s earlier Canadian settlement.

current-toronto-water.supported: City treats/tests Lake Ontario water and supplies/distributes it through its system.
current-toronto-water.limits: Only introductory source/provider/practice facts; no treatment-chemistry mastery, universalCanadianservice, every-home access or current-advice/drinking test. Use the appropriate locally verified provider for another present-day case.

current-nipissing.use: Retain already reviewed dated Nation/MOU fishery-management/reporting evidence and its contemporary-but-dated limits; no ancient direct-line identity or exact 2026legal-rule inference.

current-inuvialuit.use: Previously reviewed community-authored 2024voices: continuing harvest/tourism and documented coastal change/monitoring. Distinct modern community/context, not a timeless statement about every Inuit person or the same Qariaraqyuk settlement.

actions: Prepare separately dated young-person context cards across the studied cultures: a Droulers/St Lawrence village context around 1450 from the documented community food/housing evidence and attributed modern reconstruction; the actual Qilakitsoq young-person clothing evidence around 1475 in Greenland; and the Egyptian young-person/ordinary-life material with exact New Kingdom versus Roman-period labels. Different regional, cultural, material and social backgrounds are actual comparison dimensions, not one generic ancient child.

Label the evidence basis. Droulers food/longhouse evidence supports a cautious reconstruction of the community setting in which young people lived; it does not provide a documented individual timetable, gender duty or schooling rule. The Greenland museum directly identifies young people and clothing but does not record their complete day. Nebamun’s represented family belongs to an idealised wealthy official’s tomb context; Karanis objects are Roman-period and not evidence of that same 1350 BCE household. Fictional explanatory profiles may organise supported facts but are never presented as named real historical biographies or additional primary sources.

Have the learner identify non-sensitive actual aspects of their own daily life or class participation, such as a known shared game, food/material item, clothing or familiar building setting. Use what is actually true and freely chosen; do not presume a particular family, wealth, diet, technology or home. No address, identity record, photograph or private family history is collected. A fictional modern child cannot substitute for the required own-life connection.

Compare the chosen actual present-day aspects with supported aspects of young lives in all three early cultural settings. Explain meaningful similarities and differences using actual case facts and label any inference from general community material. Where an age, wealth or region difference may explain a contrast, do not attribute it solely to all people in an era. Do not fill unknown education, occupation or gender practices with a stereotype.

Check the whole learned early-community and Egyptian knowledge independently as already specified. The source comparison is an additional actual operation: knowing a crop or an old toy alone does not demonstrate a comparison with the learner’s own life. Use a changed attributed detail or another verified young-person context for supported transfer, and retain the evidence limits.
young-person-then-own.positive: Compares actual own daily life with supported young-person contexts from the required early cultural backgrounds. Explicitly identifies the First Nation profile as a reconstruction from community-material evidence rather than an individual record, keeps the Greenland/Egyptian dates and context distinct, and does not invent unknown daily routines.
nearMiss: Invents a modern or historical biography instead of using actual own experience and supported past context.
Uses one generic primitive child or presents every source image as an ordinary household.
Assigns specific gender/school/work duties that the source does not establish.
Backdates Roman-period toys or an undated traditional practice to a precise 1450 day.
Treats the Droulers reconstructed young-person profile as a directly documented individual daily routine, or supplies a specific school/gender timetable absent from its evidence.
young-person-then-own.sourceBoundaryForReview: The First Nation young-person comparison uses explicitly qualified community-material reconstruction, not direct individual-child documentation. This is a concrete source-fit decision to review, not a demand for learner observations.

nearMissProbes.nextMove: Identify what the source actually preserves and qualify the reconstructed setting.

nearMissProbes.nextMove: Return to the particular place, date and limited clothing evidence.

actions: Use the complete existing early material/environment profiles across Droulers, Qariaraqyuk and the dated Egyptian cases. Compare supported relations with local water, food, materials and seasonal rhythms; no every-example spiritual or religious inventory is inferred from the source’s examples.

Prepare contemporary Canadian comparison evidence using the actual current Toronto water-provider account, dated Nipissing fishery work and community-authored Tuktuuyaqtuuq account. Each remains a particular case with its own date, place and people; it does not define all Canadians, all First Nations or all Inuit. A verified local replacement may be used, retaining actual provider/community attribution and the required comparison.

Identify shared needs and supported continuing practices, such as obtaining food/water and coordinating care for resources. Explain actual differences in how the selected early settings and contemporary cases use, manage or supply those resources: documented earlier cultivation/harvest/storage and materials versus current municipal treatment/distribution or the dated fishery monitoring/management. Describe the relationship, not only list an artefact or technology.

Include the source-backed seasonal/environment connections and the contemporary practice’s purpose/limits. Do not assert that early peoples lacked governance, always lived sustainably, or that a present project proved complete environmental recovery. The present Nation/community is not labelled the direct descendant of an earlier archaeological case without its own support.

Give a supported cross-case similarity/difference and then test a new supplied contemporary account. Keep ancient inundation distinct from current river regulation, modern ecological reporting distinct from historic population inference, and individual choice distinct from institutional/community action. Learner moral approval or cultural pride is not the criterion.
environment-then-contemporary-canada.positive: Compares actual early environmental relationships and selected contemporary Canadian practices using supported similarities/differences and source/community/date limits.
nearMiss: Names ancient resources and a current city without comparing practices.
Ranks one culture as naturally better, worse or primitive.
Projects current laws, technology or community membership onto a specific early village.
Treats an announced or partial restoration project as proven universal ecological success.

limits: Whole source-fit authoring design is not a child-performance study or learner-state operation.

The explicitly qualified material-context reconstruction can support the mandatory young-person comparison; it is not an individual biography or proof of every historical routine. Success requires that distinction.
The organisation claim, governance/social-group comparisons and Inuit conflict-resolution condition remain separate.
